title: Subrectangle Queries
statement:
Design a class `SubrectangleQueries` that holds a grid of integers and lets you overwrite whole rectangular blocks of it and read single cells back.

- `SubrectangleQueries(rectangle)` stores the grid `rectangle`, which has `rows` rows and `cols` columns.
- `updateSubrectangle(row1, col1, row2, col2, newValue)` sets every cell `(r, c)` with `row1 <= r <= row2` and `col1 <= c <= col2` to `newValue`. So `(row1, col1)` is the top-left corner of the block and `(row2, col2)` its bottom-right corner, both included.
- `getValue(row, col)` returns the number the cell in row `row` and column `col` holds right now, after all earlier updates.
constraints: At most 500 calls in total are made to updateSubrectangle and getValue

signature.name: SubrectangleQueries
methods: void updateSubrectangle(int row1, int col1, int row2, int col2, int newValue)

notes:
## Intuition

The grid is at most 100 by 100 and there are at most 500 calls, so simply writing the new value into every cell of the block is cheap: even 500 full-grid updates are only 5 million writes. Once the grid always holds the current values, reading a cell is a direct lookup. (Another way is to log each update and, on a read, scan the log from newest to oldest for the first block that covers the cell; that makes updates O(1) but reads slower.)

## Approach

1. In the constructor, copy `rectangle` into `grid` so the caller's array is never changed behind its back.
2. `updateSubrectangle`: loop `row` from `row1` to `row2` and `col` from `col1` to `col2`, both ends included, and write `newValue` into each cell.
3. `getValue`: return `grid[row][col]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`grid` starts as `[[1,2,1],[4,3,4],[3,2,1],[1,1,1]]`. `getValue(0, 2)` reads `1`. `updateSubrectangle(0, 0, 3, 2, 5)` covers rows 0 to 3 and columns 0 to 2, the whole grid, so every cell becomes `5`; `getValue(0, 2)` and `getValue(3, 1)` both return `5`. `updateSubrectangle(3, 0, 3, 2, 10)` only touches row 3, which becomes `[10,10,10]`. Now `getValue(3, 1)` returns `10` and `getValue(0, 2)` still returns `5`. The results are `[null,1,null,5,5,null,10,5]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O((row2 - row1 + 1) * (col2 - col1 + 1)) per update, since each cell of the block is written once; O(1) per read.
- Space: O(rows * cols) for the copied grid.

## Pitfalls

- Both corners are inclusive: loop with `<=`, or the last row and column of the block are missed.
- The corners are `(row1, col1)` and `(row2, col2)`; mixing the argument order up (for example treating the second argument as `row2`) updates the wrong block.
- Later updates overwrite earlier ones only where the blocks overlap; cells outside the new block keep whatever value they had.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `grid` | the current values of every cell |
| `row`, `col` | the cell being written in an update, or the cell being read |
| `row1`, `col1` | top-left corner of the block to update |
| `row2`, `col2` | bottom-right corner of the block (inclusive) |
| `newValue` | the value written into every cell of the block |
